speaker: Daniela Lamas
title: THE QUARANTINE TAPES: Daniela Lamas 011
question: In hospital medicine, why does crisis resource rationing remain so difficult for bedside doctors even when a separate triage officer makes the call?
guest: Even if you're not the person making the decision, this person is your patient, and I still think it must feel a way that I never want to feel. As a doctor, you are used to making the best decision for your patient. We don't generally make decisions with the good of the broader public in mind. I don't say, 'I'm not going to give you this antibiotic because we might be running short.' No, I say, 'I'm going to give you this antibiotic; it's the right antibiotic for you.' So the idea that we would be carrying forward decisions that are really for the good of the public and not necessarily the individual is a real challenge, and something that I hope does not come to pass.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Separating the triage decision from the bedside removes the formal conflict of interest, but it does not remove the clinician's moral and practical involvement.

The bedside doctor's professional identity is built on a duty of fidelity to the individual patient, whereas crisis standards of care shift the goal to maximising population benefit. A triage officer can decide, but the treating physician still has to live with a decision that violates their own sense of what the patient is owed. That is a classic source of moral distress: knowing what you believe is right and being constrained from doing it.

They also remain the ones who carry out the decision. They supply the clinical information that drives it, tell the family, withdraw or withhold the ventilator or ICU bed, manage the dying patient's symptoms, and absorb the family's grief and anger. Often they must do this without being able to offer an appeal or alternative.

Added to this are prognostic uncertainty, scoring tools that feel crude or inequitable, lingering fears of legal liability, and inconsistent protocols. Together these mean the burden is shared but never truly lifted.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Separating triage officers from bedside clinicians is meant to protect the doctor-patient relationship, yet it removes only the formal decision, not the clinical, relational, or ethical fallout. Bedside doctors are trained and ethically bound to advocate solely for the patient in front of them, creating acute moral distress when crisis rules subordinate individual care to population-level survival. While a blinded triage officer applies standardized prognostic scores from a distance, the bedside physician knows the patient as a person, sees clinical nuances that rigid scoring tools miss, supplies the underlying clinical data, and may doubt the accuracy or fairness of the verdict. Above all, the bedside doctor must still carry the decision out: delivering devastating news to grieving or angry families, absorbing their distrust, physically withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, and witnessing an otherwise preventable decline. Because clinicians cannot simply switch off their sense of personal responsibility when enacting an irreversible outcome, offloading the choice often trades the burden of deciding for a painful mix of helplessness and felt complicity.

noweb.answer: Separating triage officers from bedside clinicians is meant to prevent conflicts of interest and reduce moral distress, yet it rarely eases the burden at the bedside. Fundamentally, physicians are trained in a fiduciary ethic: an unwavering duty to advocate for the individual patient in front of them. Crisis rationing imposes a utilitarian, population-level framework that feels like a betrayal of their core professional identity, even when someone else makes the call. Moreover, while a triage officer decides on paper, the bedside doctor must carry out that decision in the room. They are the ones who must tell terrified patients or anguished families that life-saving care is being denied, physically withhold or withdraw life support, and witness the resulting death. Finally, bedside clinicians supply the clinical assessments used for triage and see subtle individual nuances that rigid, imperfect scoring tools often miss. Enforcing an irreversible decision they may clinically doubt—against a person they have bonded with and fought to save—inflicts profound moral injury that administrative distance cannot erase.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A separate triage officer helps, but it doesn't remove the bedside doctor's role in rationing. The model exists to protect the doctor's duty to the individual patient by handing allocation decisions to someone who doesn't treat that patient. Even so, the bedside doctor still carries out the decision. They are the one who withdraws a ventilator, withholds an ICU transfer, explains the decision to a frightened family, and then cares for that patient through decline or death. Taking away the choice doesn't take away the action or its consequences.

Several other pressures make it harder. Crisis standards are built for the population, while clinical training is built around advocating for the person in front of you, so applying them feels like betraying that person and can cause moral distress or moral injury. Doctors also know the scoring tools are imperfect. SOFA scores, for example, predict poorly for individual patients and can put people with disabilities, chronic illness or from minority groups at a disadvantage. Bedside clinicians are also exhausted and often unsure of their legal protection. Finally, protocols seldom cover every situation, so doctors are left making many small rationing calls that no officer reviews.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Separating triage decisions from bedside care is meant to protect clinicians from conflicts of interest, yet it does not shield them from the moral and emotional weight of rationing. Bedside doctors still carry out the decision—withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining support from a patient they have been actively fighting to save—and they are the ones who must break the news to devastated families and witness the resulting death. Because physicians are trained under a deep fiduciary duty to prioritize the individual patient in front of them, enforcing a population-level allocation rule triggers intense moral distress, especially when they disagree with the call or doubt the precision of triage scoring systems. Moreover, bedside clinicians are rarely fully detached from the process: they supply the clinical assessments and prognostic data the triage officer relies on, which can make them feel complicit in the outcome. In practice, delegating the verdict removes the formal authority to choose, but it leaves the human burden of execution, grief, and perceived betrayal squarely at the bedside.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A separate triage officer can decide who gets a scarce ICU bed or ventilator, but the bedside doctor still has to care for the patient who goes without it. The doctor may have to explain the decision to the patient or family, withhold or withdraw treatment they believe could help, and manage the patient’s suffering. Prognosis is uncertain, which can make it especially hard to accept that a patient who might survive with treatment will go without it.

Separating the roles gives the triage officer a chance to weigh the needs of all patients consistently. The bedside doctor still owes a duty to the patient in front of them and has to act on a decision they may disagree with. That gap between what the doctor believes the patient needs and what they can provide is a source of moral distress.
